{{short description|British pathologist}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
{{More footnotes needed|date=October 2015}}

'''Dame Julia Margaret Polak''' (26 June 1939 – 11 August 2014)<ref name=Obituary>{{cite news|title=Professor Dame Julia Polak - obituary|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/11082090/Professor-Dame-Julia-Polak-obituary.html|publisher=The Telegraph|accessdate=8 September 2014|date=8 September 2014}}</ref> was an Argentine-born British [[pathologist]] who lived in England. She was head of the Centre for Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine at [[Imperial College London]], a centre for medical research she set up with Larry Hench, also from Imperial College, to develop cells and tissues for transplantation into humans.

==Biography==
Julia Polak was born in [[Buenos Aires]], [[Argentina]], daughter of Carlos Polak, a judge, and writer Rebeca Mactas Alpersohn. Her family was Jewish, and had fled persecution in Eastern Europe.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(14)61809-2 | title=Julia Margaret Polak | journal=The Lancet | date=11 October 2014 | volume=384 | issue=9951 | page=1342 | last1=Laurance | first1=Jeremy | pmid=25317447 | s2cid=33092517 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.scotsman.com/news/obituaries/obituary-professor-dame-julia-polak-histochemist-1525904 | title=Obituary: Professor Dame Julia Polak, histochemist | date=19 September 2014 }}</ref> She was educated at the [[University of Buenos Aires]], before moving to London. She was married to a fellow student, Daniel Catovsky, and had three children.<ref name="Munk's">{{cite web |title=Julia Margaret (Dame) Polak |url=http://munksroll.rcplondon.ac.uk/Biography/Details/6977 |website=Munks Roll |publisher=Royal College of Physicians of London |accessdate=2 March 2019 |archive-date=6 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306042640/http://munksroll.rcplondon.ac.uk/Biography/Details/6977 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Her grand-niece is American model and actress [[Camila Morrone]].{{citation needed|date=August 2022}}

Polak was one of the longest surviving recipients of a [[heart and lung transplant]] in the [[United Kingdom]]. It was her transplant in 1995 which caused her to change her career direction from [[pathology]] towards the newly developing field of [[tissue engineering]].

She was editor of the journal, ''Tissue Engineering'', as well as a member of the MRC/UK Stem Cell Bank Clinical and User Liaison Committee and an advisor to the Science and Parliament Committees. She was recognized as one of the most highly cited and influential researchers in her field.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://highlycited.com/categories/clinical_medicine/|title=Clinical Medicine category list|work=[[ISIHighlyCited.com]]|accessdate=18 May 2012}}</ref>

Her work was recognized by the Society for Endocrinology, the International Academy of Pathology and the Association of Clinical Pathologists. She received funding through the Texas/United Kingdom Collaborative Research Initiative in Biosciences. {{Citation needed|date=September 2010}}

Polak died on 11 August 2014, aged 75, from undisclosed causes.<ref name=Obituary/>

==Awards and honours==
In the [[2003 Queen's Birthday Honours]], she was made [[List of Dames Commander of the Order of the British Empire|Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (DBE) for her services to medicine. She was elected a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] in 1999.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Deceased Fellows |url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/more-fellowship/deceased-fellows |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=Academy of Medical Sciences}}</ref> In 2004, she received the [[Ellison-Cliffe Lecture|Ellison-Cliffe Medal]] from the [[Royal Society of Medicine]].
